cards.front: List the access levels from most open to most restrictive.
cards.extra: Package access is what you get when you write nothing. Each level adds another group of code that can see the member.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::03 Access Modifiers
cards.example:
public class Ex {
    public int a; protected int b; int c; private int d;
    public static void main(String[] x) { Ex e = new Ex(); System.out.println(e.a + e.b + e.c + e.d); }
}

cards.front: What is package access, and how do you request it?
cards.back: Visibility to classes in the same package only — you request it by writing no modifier
cards.extra: It is the default, not a keyword. In practice it means "this is an internal detail shared by the package".
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::03 Access Modifiers
cards.example:
package demo;
class PackagePrivate { int x = 1; }
public class Ex { public static void main(String[] a) { System.out.println(new PackagePrivate().x); } }

cards.front: Why does Java have access control at all?
cards.back: To separate the parts that may change from the parts clients depend on
cards.extra: A library author must be able to rewrite internals without breaking callers. Without specifiers, every field you expose is frozen forever.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::03 Access Modifiers
cards.example:
class Library {
    private int mayChange = 1;   // implementation detail, free to change
    public int api() { return mayChange; }  // the part clients depend on
}
class Client { int use(Library l) { return l.api(); } }

cards.front: What does protected add to package access?
cards.back: Access from subclasses, even in another package
cards.extra: It is the only level that reaches across packages by inheritance. protected plus package access together are why the level feels unusual.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::03 Access Modifiers
cards.example:
class Base { protected int n = 1; }
class Sub extends Base { int read() { return n; } }  // subclass in another package still sees n
class Peer { int peer(Base b) { return b.n; } }  // same package: the package-access part

cards.front: What does the package statement do, and where must it go?
cards.back: Declares the library unit the class belongs to; it must be the first statement in the file
cards.extra: The package name becomes part of the class's fully qualified name and matches the directory structure. One file can declare only one package.
cards.example:
package demo;
public class Ex { public static void main(String[] a) { System.out.println("in demo"); } }

cards.front: A class has no package statement. Where does it live?
cards.extra: Fine for experiments, impossible to import from a named package. Production code always declares one.
cards.example:
// no package statement at the top of the file
class NoPackage { int n = 1; }   // lives in the unnamed (default) package
